title: What and how hospital chaplains contribute to the spiritual care of palliative patients
summary:
When people become seriously ill, they often have spiritual needs. These may include questions about the meaning of their illness, illness-related and other worries and needs that need to be discussed, a desire to look back on their lives, and much more. These and similar topics are often discussed in conversations with hospital chaplains. The study is being conducted to gain insights through interviews into how conversations with hospital chaplains help palliative care patients with their spiritual needs.
The interviews with the hospital chaplains accompanying palliative care patients are intended to provide insights into whether the level of reflection or qualification of the hospital chaplain has an impact on the effectiveness of the pastoral care conversation.

interventions.name: During their stay in hospital, patients have the opportunity to talk to hospital chaplains. Patients who are either in a palliative care unit or receiving palliative care in another unit and who have had one or more conversations with a hospital chaplain are eligible for the study. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Inclusion criteria for patients:
-    A signed declaration of consent
-    Adult palliative care patients in the rehabilitation and 
(pre-) terminal phase who are capable of giving consent and whose limitations allow them to be interviewed

Inclusion criteria for pastoral caregivers:
-    One or more conversations with the interviewed patient
-    Clinical Pastoral Education (CPE) or CPE-equivalent training or CPE or CPE-equivalent training and subject-specific further training
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion criteria for patients:
- Minors or patients incapable of giving consent
- Patients in the late terminal phase
- Patients in the final phase
- Non-German-speaking patients (language skills)
- Patients with cognitive impairments

Exclusion criteria for pastoral caregivers:
- No guided conversation with an interviewed patient
- No clinical pastoral education (CPE)
